requirements.requirement: /tmp is mounted with noexec, nosuid, and nodev (program execution, setuid, and device nodes all ignored)
requirements.summary: Baseline showed /tmp not separately mounted (cmd-e6f8df2daca14695). Executor added a bind mount in fstab and remounted live, findmnt confirmed rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec on /tmp (cmd-a6491a15c0244f39). Functional proof: script execution denied (exit 126), mknod device write denied, and a copied setuid binary failed to execute (cmd-315d07239a944545, cmd-47ff7acf544b4659, cmd-91629e037f2d4825).

requirements.requirement: /dev/shm is mounted with noexec, nosuid, and nodev
requirements.summary: Baseline showed /dev/shm mounted with only nosuid,nodev (no noexec) (cmd-e6f8df2daca14695, cmd-5e9047c7f6174bb7). Executor added noexec to the tmpfs mount via fstab and remount; findmnt confirmed rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec (cmd-a6491a15c0244f39). Functional tests confirmed exec, device, and setuid execution are all blocked on /dev/shm (cmd-315d07239a944545, cmd-47ff7acf544b4659).

fstab entries were added persistently for /tmp and /dev/shm (cmd-5aae1ce9b0a54d1e). Pre-reboot boot_id and mount state were captured (cmd-0fadd283587a47d9, boot_id 513c865e...), a reboot was issued and acknowledged (cmd-51fb45bb5a984edb), the node was unreachable during the transition (cmd-80d6d89f03fc4d92, cmd-4385718c0c444d4c, cmd-52a451d373c84fca), then reconnected with a new boot_id 69a35f84... (cmd-adc1c053a30b46cf), matching the fixed after_executor boot-identity snapshot. Post-reboot findmnt and repeated exec/device functional tests confirmed both mounts retained nosuid,nodev,noexec (cmd-bb4fe681ffeb4537).

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task — noexec/nosuid/nodev enforcement on /tmp, the same on /dev/shm, and persistence across a real reboot — are directly and coherently demonstrated with pre-change baseline, applied configuration, functional proof (execution, device node, and setuid all blocked), a genuine reboot (boot_id changed from 513c865e... to 69a35f84..., matching the fixed lifecycle snapshots), and post-reboot re-verification showing the hardening survived. Hygiene is very good; the only blemishes are a small leftover log file and a retained fstab backup, both low-risk and non-conflicting with system state.
limitations: No independent access to live systems; assessment relies entirely on captured command output and fixed lifecycle snapshots.

The provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol coincides with the task's own required reboot for node1 (the only managed node), so no additional restart evidence beyond what satisfies the task itself was available to cross-check separately.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were tightly scoped to the task: baseline discovery (cmd-e6f8df2daca14695, cmd-5e9047c7f6174bb7), fstab backup before edit (cmd-5aae1ce9b0a54d1e), live remount to apply settings (cmd-a6491a15c0244f39), functional verification with temporary test artifacts (scripts, device nodes, a setuid binary copy) that were explicitly removed after each check (cmd-315d07239a944545, cmd-47ff7acf544b4659, cmd-91629e037f2d4825, cmd-bb4fe681ffeb4537), and a single reboot used to prove persistence (cmd-51fb45bb5a984edb). No unnecessary or unexplained mutations were found; no failed services or altered listening sockets resulted (only expected pid/boot_id changes from the reboot per the fixed after_executor snapshot). Two minor residues remain: /tmp/reboot.log (redirect target of the backgrounded reboot command, cmd-51fb45bb5a984edb) is visible in the after_executor temporary-files snapshot and was not cleaned up, and the /etc/fstab.bak.<timestamp> backup file (cmd-5aae1ce9b0a54d1e) was intentionally retained as a safety backup rather than cleaned. Both are low-risk, bounded, and plausibly justified (backup) or trivial (a log file), so hygiene is scored high but not perfect.
